observations: The strongest chronologies use a repeated secret as pressure that changes questions, concessions, or disclosure; the weakest merely restate the secret and permission clause every turn.

A public mannerism remains useful when reflection exposes what it protects and lets that interior alter later behavior. It fails when performance, correction, procedural care, or silence becomes the entire character.

Hard failures came from packet-level contradictions or invented continuity: a wrong guess treated as correct, a mother alert conflated with Haruki's message, six ordinary days rewritten as disappearance, inconsistent pronouns, and a silence sequence with no private motive.
Continued nondisclosure was not penalized when an authorization or undecided-choice boundary remained active and the chronology still developed relationally.
Relationship/status cost was usually present, but it was often the easiest field to fill generically; it became discriminating only when later turns changed who bore the cost or what action followed.
